Achieve Full GPU Utilization Cut GPU costs by 70% Maximize model performance Free your engineers Book a Demo Kubernetes DRA GPU enforcement is the set of controls that decide what a workload may hold and what it may consume on an accelerator. Dynamic Resource Allocation governs the first half at scheduling time and delegates the second half entirely to the vendor driver. That is why a container can be granted 20 GiB and use 60 GiB without Kubernetes noticing. Why Kubernetes DRA GPU enforcement is harder than it looks I spent three days getting DRA working on a fresh Kubernetes 1.36 cluster, in August 2026. Not three days of deep work. Three days of hitting things the release notes did not mention, the kind that only become obvious once you have seen the exact error. A few of them, and I am naming versions because several have since expired. The feature gate named in half the documentation, DRAResourceClaimStatus , did not exist on 1.36.0, and the real one was DRAResourceClaimDeviceStatus . The Helm OCI path for the NVIDIA DRA driver was broken on Helm 3.20 and later, so you needed the NGC repo instead. MPS sharing worked, but only after you flipped a gate that defaulted to false in the chart. Device health stayed Unknown until you flipped another one. Eleven of those, all on a clean install from the current docs, written up with the exact flags in the 1.36 defaults-flip piece , where the MPS gate is gotcha number four. Check those against your own version before quoting them at me. Kubernetes 1.37 graduated ResourceClaim device status and pod resource health status to stable, which retires the gate-name trap and the Unknown health reading entirely. The 1.37 walkthrough covers what closed. Those are install problems. They cost an afternoon each and then they are solved forever, because somebody writes them down. This article is about the one that is not an install problem, and I did not recognize it as different until I tried to measure it. The same shape kept appearing: a default that reads as enabled, publishing nothing, until a second flag somewhere else turns it on. At the install layer that is an annoyance. At the layer this article is about, it is the whole architecture, and no flag fixes it. Here is what that looks like from a distance. Somebody on your team has a dashboard open right now showing an H100 fleet at comfortable utilization. Every claim satisfied, no pending pods, no allocation errors. That dashboard is telling the truth. It is also, in a specific and expensive way, not answering the question anyone actually asked. Dynamic Resource Allocation reached GA in Kubernetes v1.34 and has been stable and enabled by default since v1.35. It fixed something that badly needed fixing. Under the device plugin model a GPU was an opaque integer, and the scheduler had no way to reason about memory, model, or interconnect. You asked for one GPU and hoped. DRA replaced that with a typed request language and a durable record of what was granted to whom. That record is sound. The scheduler will not grant more of a device than the device advertises. Consumable capacity extends the same arithmetic to fractions of a card, and the Kubernetes gate for it is on by default in 1.36. Be careful what that means: the gate is scheduler arithmetic, and it does nothing at all until a driver actually publishes consumable capacity. A hands-on look at Kubernetes 1.37 resource management. Every finding below was reproduced on kubeadm v1.37.0, on freshly built clusters, in August 2026. Grab a pan handle that has been sitting over a low flame and your hand is back at your side before you understand why. That is a reflex arc: a stimulus, a nerve, a muscle, no brain in the loop. It saves the hand in about fifty milliseconds. It also puts dinner across the kitchen floor, because a reflex protects exactly one thing and knows nothing about what else you were holding. I spent two weeks inside the 1.37 binaries, and most of it went the way lab time goes. The kind node image did not exist yet, so the plan changed to kubeadm on day one. Kubernetes 1.37 is where the kernel grows reflexes. The release team named this one Garhwal , after a Himalayan region of Uttarakhand, and described the logo’s terraced fields as climbing toward the peaks with “each level supported by the one below.” That is a fair description of this series too. 1.35 shipped the syscalls, 1.36 turned the defaults on, and 1.37 is the level built on both. Kubernetes 1.37 resource management is the release where the cluster starts reacting to the syscalls it shipped in 1.35 and 1.36. Resize can preempt. The pod-scope resource model fills out. DRA gets an adoption bridge for existing nvidia.com/gpu requests. Workload-Aware Scheduling moves into beta, and HPA finally scales to zero, for Object and External metrics only. And like the hand leaving the pan, these arcs fire without a brain attached: upstream’s own documentation states that resize preemption bypasses node affinity, pod anti-affinity, and topology spread. Achieve Full GPU Utilization Cut GPU costs by 70% Maximize model performance Free your engineers Book a Demo Running AI agents on Kubernetes means hosting long-lived, stateful agent processes as workloads on a cluster. In most production deployments the agent process and the GPU are in different pods. The agent itself is orchestration logic, tool definitions, and session state, usually built with a framework like LangChain or LlamaIndex, and it is CPU-only. The GPU sits in a separate inference tier, a runtime such as vLLM or NVIDIA Triton, serving many agents at once behind an HTTP endpoint. A smaller set of deployments loads the model inside the agent’s own container, so a single process holds both the orchestration logic and the model weights with no serving layer in between. That arrangement changes which of the fixes below apply, and the difference is flagged at each point where it matters. The hidden cost is the same in both arrangements. GPU capacity is reserved for the lifetime of the pod holding it, agent demand arrives in bursts, and Kubernetes has no native signal that tells it the accelerator is sitting idle between tasks. In a split deployment that idle capacity is spread across every inference deployment serving the fleet, which in a multi-model stack means a main model, a routing or classification model, an embedding model, and a re-ranker, each reserving its own accelerator and each with its own duty cycle. Most teams run inference capacity always-on by default when the workload shape argues for inference-aware replica scaling, and the resulting idle-GPU bill is the largest and most invisible line item in an agent platform. We are not going to argue it from first principles. We built the fleet, measured it, and broke it on purpose. What we measured. We measured the idle fleet, then turned ScaleOps automation on and captured what it reclaimed. The synthetic workload holds its model in the same container as the agent logic, with no inference server in front of it, so the figures describe a single-tenant deployment where the weights are the entire GPU memory footprint. Where a result depends on that arrangement, we say so at the point of use. Full methodology is at the end.
